In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of Ca2+ as an intracellular second messenger in the cerebellar granule cells.
the role of Ca2+ in the function of cerebellar granule neurones, the main excitatory neurons of the cerebellum.
the mechanisms underlying [Ca2+] i signalling in granule cell neurones.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the [Ca2+] transients in granule neurone are generated by a complex interplay of voltage-gated, glutamate-gated and intracellular store-operated plasmalemmally located Ca2+ channels.
the [Ca2+] i signal in granule neurone is generated predominantly by Ca2+ influx through plasmalemmall Ca2+ channels.

in neonatal cerebellar neurones the [Ca2+]I transients evoked by K(+)-depolarization, caffeine or glutamate application are due to Ca(2+) influx via different voltage-gated channels, Ca2+ release from intracellular stores (via ryanodine-sensitive Ca(2+)) and Ca(2+) release from internal stores via inositol (1,4, 5)-tris-phosphate-sensitive mechanisms.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
in neonatal granule cells, Ca2+ signalling is dominated by Ca2+ release from intracellular Ca2+ stores, while in mature granule cells Ca2+ influx dominates the Ca2+ signalling.
the [Ca2+]I transients in granule neurone are mainly due to influx of Ca2+ through voltage-gated Ca(2+) channels and glutamate-gates channels.
the granule neurones from neonates and adults express different types of plasmalemal Ca2+ channels and different types of Ca2+ stores.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the mechanisms of Ca2+ signalling in granule cells are developmentally regulated.
in cerebellar granule cells, the [Ca2+]I signal is generated mainly through plasmalemmally located Ca2+ entry mechanisms.
the Ca2+ signalling in cerebellar granule neurones is complex and involves several different mechanisms of Ca2+ influx into the cell.
